newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems, Croats agree power-sharing deal for city.
newsitem.headline: Moslems, Croats agree power-sharing deal for city.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem and Croat leaders agreed late on Thursday on a power-sharing deal for Sarajevo's city government, paving way for the election of a mayor for the Bosnian capital, state television reported.
Sarajevo has had no mayor for more than a year due to months of political stalemate.

International mediators have been calling on local leaders to put aside their differences over power-sharing and throw their support behind a prominent figure as mayor that could promote the city's reconstruction.
"The aim of today's agreement is electing the city mayor," Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, said after the agreement was reached.
"The mayor must be a person respected in wider spheres, who will support the multi-ethnic character of Sarajevo," Steiner said. He did not name that person.
Sarajevo once had large Serb and Croat minorities but after the 1992-95 Bosnian war, the city is now predominantly Moslem.

Croats are estimated to comprise less than 10 percent of the city's post-war population. All but a few Serbs fled in the Spring of 1996 when their suburbs reverted to the Moslem-Croat federation control.

The last mayor of Sarajevo, Tarik Kupusovic, a Moslem, resigned last year in protest over political moves by his own party, the nationalist Moslem Party of Democratic Action (SDA), which he said raised political tensions.
The argument over the structure of Sarajevo's city government has been one of many disputes that has plagued Bosnia's troubled Moslem-Croat federation.
Croats suspect Moslem leaders of trying to dominate the federation based on a larger share of the population.
Moslems have accused Croats of plotting to annex Croat-controlled territory to neighbouring Croatia.
A 1995 peace treaty preserved Bosnia as a single state comprised of the federation and a Serb entity.

If the agreement is implemented, the mayor is supposed to be elected at the inaugural session of the city council scheduled for April 10 -- two days before Pope John Paul II makes a historic visit to Sarajevo.
